trajectory.response:
I have everything from the Revenue Department's own English pages. Here is the full picture.

## Sources used (all rd.go.th English)
| Page | Last updated |
|---|---|
| Personal Income Tax (PIT), `/english/6045.0.html` | 21.03.2024 |
| Tax Clearance Certificate, `/english/23518.html` | 23.11.2020 |
| Rights and Duties of a Taxpayer | — |
| RD news item "How do foreigners living in Thailand pay tax?" (PDF, `FOREIGNERS_PAY_TAX2024.pdf`), posted 24 Sep 2024 | 2024 |

---

## 1. The two triggers: how long you stay, and whether you remit

The PIT page, §1 "Taxable Person":

> "'Resident' means any person residing in Thailand for a period or periods aggregating **more than 180 days in any tax (calendar) year**. A resident of Thailand is liable to pay tax on income from sources in Thailand as well as on the portion of income from foreign sources **that is brought into Thailand**. A non-resident is, however, subject to tax only on income from sources in Thailand."

So there are two independent switches:

- **Day-count (180 days, per calendar year, not rolling).** Days need not be consecutive — "a period or periods aggregating." Cross 180 in a calendar year and you are resident *for that whole year*. Reset each 1 January.
- **Remittance.** Residency alone does not tax your foreign salary. Only the **portion brought into Thailand** is taxable. Money left offshore is outside the charge.

**Your situation specifically:** your employer being abroad is irrelevant to sourcing here — what matters is that the income is foreign-sourced, so it bites only when both switches are on (resident **and** remitted). If you stay ≤180 days, foreign salary is untouched no matter how much you remit.

### The remittance timing question — resolved by the 2024 RD document
This is where the plain PIT page is silent and the 2024 news PDF is decisive. It sets out Section 41 and distinguishes:

- **Remitted in the same tax year it was earned** → assessable in that year.
- **Remitted in a later tax year** → under the RD's current position this is **still assessable, in the year of remittance**, provided you were a Thai resident in the year the income arose.
- The PDF's matrix turns on whether you were resident *in the year the income was earned* and resident *in the year of remittance*. The case that escapes: income earned in a year in which you were **not** a Thai tax resident — remitting that later does not bring it into charge.

Practical consequence: pre-arrival savings, and income from any year you were under 180 days, are the clean pool. Tag your accounts by vintage before you remit.

Two further points from that PDF:
- **Filing:** foreigners must report Thai-sourced income earned in the year *and* foreign-sourced income remitted in the year on P.N.D.90/91. "If foreign-sourced income is remitted **partially**, the taxable amount shall be **apportioned** accordingly."
- **Foreign tax relief:** tax paid abroad is creditable if a Double Tax Agreement permits, capped at the Thai tax attributable to that foreign income. Evidence must be in English or Thai; a Tax Payment Certificate from the foreign authority is recommended.

---

## 2. Figures that carry a vintage note — treat as NOT current

You were right to be suspicious. Flagging each as instructed:

**Progressive rate table (§3.1)** — 0–150,000 exempt; 5% / 10% / 15% / 20% / 25% / 30%; over 4,000,000 at 35%. Immediately beneath the table the page states:

> **"To be implemented for the 2013 and 2014 tax years."**

That note is the page's own scope limitation. **This table may no longer be current** — it is presented by the RD as applying to tax years 2013–2014, over a decade ago. Do not compute a 2026 liability from it without confirming the rates in force.

**Allowances table (§2.2)** — personal allowance **30,000 baht** (single taxpayer; 30,000 for spouse; 30,000 per partner in a non-juristic partnership capped at 60,000); spouse allowance 30,000; child allowance 15,000 each, max three children; education 2,000 per child; home mortgage interest up to 100,000; life insurance, provident fund and LTF entries as shown. This table carries **no tax-year note at all**, which is its own warning — the surrounding page is demonstrably of 2013–14 vintage, and the "Long term equity fund" line refers to a vehicle whose contribution window has since closed. **Treat these amounts as possibly superseded.**

**Withholding table (§4)** — employment income shown as **"5 – 37%"**, and non-resident public entertainer at "5 – 37%". Note this is internally inconsistent with the same page's own rate table, which tops out at **35%**. 37% was the pre-2013 top rate. **This is stale on its face.**

**Deductions table (§2.2)** — employment and copyright income: "40% but not exceeding 60,000 baht." No year note. The 40%/60,000 formulation is the older standard-deduction rule; **verify before relying on it.**

Reliable and undated on the same page: the 180-day test, the residence/remittance charging rule, and the filing deadlines. Those are structural provisions of the Revenue Code rather than annually-set numbers, which is why I'd weight them differently from the tables.

---

## 3. The tax clearance certificate: the rule vs. the exemption that swallows it

This is the page you were half-remembering, and the answer is that **the exemption governs — it almost certainly does not apply to you.**

**The rule (§2), stated broadly:**
> "Section 4 quarter of the Revenue Code stipulates that **a foreigner departing shall apply for a Tax Clearance Certificate** in the form prescribed by the Director-General **within 15 days before leaving the country, whether or not there is any tax payable**."

Read alone, that sounds universal. But the same section then narrows it to three cases, and §3 nullifies the general sweep.

**The exemption (§3), which controls:**
> "In addition the Revenue Department issued the **Notification of the Director-General of the Revenue Department on 7 May 1991** stipulating that **foreigners departing Thailand do not have to apply for a Tax Clearance Certificate except for the above three cases in 2.**"

§3 also carves out, under Section 4 quarter itself, a foreigner "transiting Thailand, or entering or residing in Thailand for a period or periods aggregating **not more than 90 days** in a tax year without earning assessable income."

**Which governs:** the 1991 Director-General's Notification. The default flips from "everyone must" to "**nobody must, unless you fall in one of three buckets**." Those three, verbatim from §2:

1. He is **liable to payment of tax or tax arrears** before departing Thailand;
2. He has a **duty to file a tax return and pay tax on behalf of a company or juristic partnership incorporated under foreign laws** and carrying on business in Thailand;
3. He has **taxable income from being a public performer** in Thailand, whether or not earned in Thailand. ("Public performer" = drama, movie, radio/TV performer, singer, musician, professional sportsperson or entertainer.)

**Applied to you:** a remote employee of a foreign company is **not** bucket 2 — that bucket is about acting as the filing agent for a foreign company doing business in Thailand, not about merely being employed by one. You are not bucket 3. You would only be caught by **bucket 1**, and only if you have assessed tax or arrears actually outstanding at the moment of departure. Pay on time and no clearance certificate is required. Note the 90-day carve-out will not help you personally — it requires *both* ≤90 days *and* no assessable income.

**If bucket 1 ever does apply:** Form P.1, filed within 15 days before departure with the Area Revenue Office for your area of residence. Two certificate types — **P.3** (single departure, valid 15 days from issuance, renewable before expiry) and **P.3.1** (multiple departures for a regular business/professional traveller, valid up to 180 days from issuance, **renewal not allowed**).
